content: The evaluation of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) published up to May 2010 was conducted using predefined data search strategies. In addition to database searches, bibliographies of reviews and guidelines were examined, citations of all included studies were screened, and experts in the field, as well as IGRA manufacturers, were contacted to identify additional studies, including published, unpublished, and ongoing research. Relevant information not reported in the original publications was requested from the primary authors of all studies included in the systematic review. Studies assessing the performance of commercially available IGRAs, published in any language and conducted in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), were reviewed by specific topics. The analysis included studies on the performance of IGRAs in LMICs, excluding those using purified protein derivative (PPD)-based IGRAs, IGRAs performed on non-blood specimens, studies focusing on the effect of anti-tuberculosis treatment on IGRA responses, studies with fewer than 10 participants, studies with insufficient data to determine diagnostic accuracy, and conference abstracts or letters without original data. Study quality was assessed using standardized methods appropriate to the topic. For test accuracy outcomes, quality was evaluated using a subset of criteria from the QUADAS tool, while for predictive value studies, a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used. Conflicts of interest were a known concern in tuberculosis (TB) diagnostic studies. The systematic reviews included a quality item addressing the involvement of commercial test manufacturers in the design or conduct of studies, including the donation of test materials, financial support, or relationships with study authors. Data synthesis and meta-analysis were conducted using a standardized approach to account for heterogeneity. Data were synthesized separately for each commercial IGRA and by World Bank income classification (LMICs versus high-income countries). Heterogeneity was assessed visually using forest plots, characterized using the I-squared statistic, and tested statistically using the chi-squared test. Pooled estimates were calculated using random-effects modeling, which is more conservative in the presence of heterogeneity. For the diagnosis of active TB, studies included those evaluating the performance of IGRAs among adults with presumed TB or confirmed TB in LMICs. The initial search identified 789 citations, and after full-text review of 185 papers, 22 studies met eligibility criteria, covering 33 unique evaluations of one or more IGRAs. Of these, 30% were from low-income countries, and 70% were from middle-income countries. Among the studies, 52% included people living with HIV (PLHIV), and 82% involved ambulatory subjects. The sensitivity of IGRAs for detecting active TB among suspected cases in LMICs ranged from 73% to 83%, while specificity ranged from 49% to 58%. This means that, on average, one in four patients with culture-confirmed active TB could be IGRA-negative, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. There was no evidence that IGRAs provided added value beyond conventional microbiological tests for diagnosing active TB. Sensitivity was lower among PLHIV (60–70%), indicating that nearly one in three PLHIV with active TB would be IGRA-negative. There was no consistent evidence that IGRAs were more sensitive than the tuberculin skin test (TST) for active TB diagnosis. Limited head-to-head comparisons suggested higher sensitivity for the T-SPOT platform compared to QFT-GIT, but the difference was not statistically significant. Specificity for active TB was low for both IGRAs, regardless of HIV status, with one in two patients without active TB being IGRA-positive, leading to unnecessary therapy and missed differential diagnoses. Operational aspects of IGRA use highlighted several challenges. The cost of IGRAs was noted as a limitation in four studies, with assays deemed too expensive. Only one study addressed reproducibility, showing excellent inter-observer agreement for T-SPOT. No studies reported on time-to-result for IGRAs. Feasibility issues included the amount of blood required, high background results in negative control tubes, and the need for well-equipped laboratories and trained personnel, which could pose logistical challenges. Research priorities include the development of IGRAs with improved accuracy, based on robust study designs with representative populations, prospective follow-up, and adequate blinding. Proof-of-principle studies should be followed by well-designed evaluation studies assessing patient impact.
